content: St. John Ambulance (SJA) in Canada is a highly respected and globally recognized non-profit organization specializing in first aid training. Its mission is to empower Canadians to enhance their health, safety, and quality of life through education and community service. History St. John Ambulance was established in Canada in 1882, with volunteers nationwide contributing to the humanitarian efforts of the Most Venerable Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem. In 1897, the Dominion Council of Canada was formed in Ottawa to formalize the operations of the St. John Ambulance Brigade. Around the same time, the Brigade began its activities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia. By 1933, the Dominion Council evolved into the Commandery of Canada due to the growing demand for first aid services and training. In 1946, the Priory of Canada of the Most Venerable Order of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem was established. This change addressed two key needs: the expanding scope of the St. John Ambulance Association and Brigade across Canada, and the necessity of transferring governance from the Priory of England and the Islands to Canada’s national capital, Ottawa. Training St. John Ambulance is a national leader in first aid education, setting the benchmark for training in first aid, CPR, and other life-saving techniques. The organization offers advanced courses, such as Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) training in several provinces, and operates the Maritime School of Paramedicine in Nova Scotia. Volunteer Brigade The St. John Ambulance Volunteer Brigade consists of highly trained volunteers who provide first aid services at public events, assist during emergencies or disasters, and participate in youth programs that promote community service and personal growth. Brigade members deliver patient care and first responder services at events across Canada. They wear uniforms similar to their counterparts in England and are trained to advanced levels, including the Medical First Responder (MFR) program. In Nova Scotia, the term Brigade or Ambulance is no longer used; instead, volunteers are referred to as St. John Volunteer Medical Response to better reflect their role in the community. Nationwide, St. John Ambulance has over 25,000 members in more than 300 communities, representing all age groups. Therapy Dog Program Recognizing the isolation faced by many individuals in hospitals, nursing homes, and other care facilities, St. John Ambulance initiated the Therapy Dog Program in Peterborough, Ontario. This program has since expanded across Canada, forming partnerships with hospitals, palliative care units, senior residences, special needs schools, and psychiatric facilities. Therapy dogs provide comfort to stroke patients, Alzheimer’s patients, and individuals with physical disabilities. For example, stroke patients may use their affected hand to pet a dog, while Alzheimer’s patients often recall fond memories of their own pets. The program involves weekly visits by volunteers and their dogs, fostering meaningful connections between the clients, the dogs, and the volunteers. We Can Help Program The We Can Help program is designed for children aged seven to ten, introducing them to basic first aid skills and injury prevention. This initiative aims to strengthen children’s understanding of safety, given the significant responsibilities they often bear. Friends of the Emergency Room The Friends of the Emergency Room program involves volunteers who provide comfort and support to patients and their companions in the emergency department of the Royal Alexandra Hospital in Alberta. These volunteers play a vital role in the emergency care team, offering emotional support and assistance in the waiting room. Youth Programs Youth members are an integral part of St. John Ambulance Canada. The proficiency program allows young participants to earn the Grand Prior’s Award and work toward the Duke of Edinburgh’s Award. Proficiencies are granted for demonstrating knowledge in various subjects, both related and unrelated to the organization. The program equips youth with valuable life skills and meets the requirements for the Grand Prior’s Award, which is achieved after completing six compulsory and six elective proficiency courses. Additionally, youth members can engage in community service and provide patient care at public events under the supervision of trained adult members. Disaster Planning and Aid During emergencies, St. John Ambulance Canada is prepared to provide disaster relief and emergency services. The specific response depends on local disaster management plans, but the Canadian government officially recognizes SJA’s role in such situations. The organization has a National Duty Officer system in place to mobilize additional personnel and equipment to support local divisions when needed. Supplies, equipment, and the number of available personnel may vary by region, but SJA is equipped to respond effectively to emergencies.
